title: SALTT vs LMNT: Which Electrolyte Mix Is Better?
excerpt: SALTT vs LMNT compared: sodium, potassium, magnesium, price, taste, and which works better for keto, workouts, or a hangover, plus who should check with a doctor first.
metaDescription: SALTT vs LMNT: sodium, potassium, magnesium, and price compared, which is better for keto, workouts, or a hangover, and who should be careful.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** SALTT and LMNT are close cousins. Both are sugar-free, stevia-sweetened electrolyte mixes with roughly a gram of sodium per stick, and both were built for people eating low-carb, fasting, or sweating hard. The real differences are in the other two minerals. A stick of SALTT has about twice the potassium of LMNT and about three times the magnesium, and it usually costs a bit less per stick. LMNT is the older, better-known brand, easier to find, and has a lighter magnesium dose that's gentler on sensitive stomachs. If you want the most minerals per dollar, SALTT is the better value. If you want the simpler, more widely available product, or magnesium tends to upset your gut, LMNT is the safer pick. For a hangover, neither one is ideal on its own, and neither one cures a hangover.

**The quick picks:**

- **Keto, low-carb, or fasting, and you want the fullest mineral dose:** SALTT.
- **Heavy sweating and you mainly want sodium:** either works. LMNT if you prefer a lower magnesium dose.
- **Sensitive stomach or you already take a magnesium supplement:** LMNT, or half a stick of SALTT.
- **Hangover with nausea or you can barely keep fluids down:** a classic oral rehydration drink with a little sugar is usually a better tool than either.
- **High blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or you take blood pressure pills:** talk to your doctor before using either one regularly.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares general label information and research. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using high-sodium, high-potassium electrolyte mixes regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, you've been told to limit salt, potassium, or fluids, or you take medicines that affect sodium or potassium levels (such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone, or other water pills). Label numbers change over time, so check the current package for exact figures.

## SALTT vs LMNT at a Glance

Here's how the standard stick versions compare. These are approximate figures from each brand's published labels at the time of writing, and they vary a little by flavor.

| | SALTT (drink mix stick) | LMNT (standard flavors) |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium | ~970 mg | ~1,000 mg |
| Potassium | ~410 mg | ~200 mg |
| Magnesium | ~180 mg | ~60 mg |
| Sugar | 0 g | 0 g |
| Sweetener | Stevia (the unflavored "Clean Slate" is unsweetened) | Stevia (the "Raw" version is unsweetened) |
| Salt source | A mineral sea-salt blend (sold as SolarSea) plus potassium chloride | Sodium chloride, potassium chloride, magnesium malate |
| Other forms | Drink mix, liquid drops, capsules | Drink mix, canned sparkling water |
| Typical price per stick | Roughly $1.20 | Roughly $1.50, less with bulk or subscription |
| Made by | Keto Chow (Utah), launched under the SALTT name in late 2023 | Drink LMNT, co-founded by Robb Wolf |

The headline: **sodium is basically a tie. SALTT gives you much more potassium and magnesium. LMNT gives you less of both and has more brand recognition.** Almost every "which one should I buy" question comes down to whether you actually want that extra potassium and magnesium.

## Where the Two Brands Come From

**LMNT** launched around 2018 and grew out of the paleo and low-carb world. Co-founder Robb Wolf is a writer and podcaster known in that space, and the product's pitch has always been that many active and low-carb people are under-salted. LMNT made the "one gram of sodium, no sugar" formula famous, and it's now one of the best-known electrolyte brands online.

**SALTT** comes from Keto Chow, a Utah company best known for keto meal-replacement shakes. Keto Chow sold its own electrolyte products for years and moved them under the SALTT name (pronounced "salty") in late 2023. The pitch is very similar to LMNT's, with two twists: more potassium and magnesium per stick, and a lower price. SALTT also sells concentrated drops and capsules, which LMNT doesn't.

Both are smaller, direct-to-consumer brands. Both sell through their own websites and Amazon. LMNT is easier to find in physical stores and gyms. Neither is a medical product, and neither is regulated the way a drug is.

## Sodium: Nearly Identical

Sodium is the electrolyte you lose most of in sweat, and it's the one that matters most for holding on to water. On this measure the two products are essentially the same. SALTT lists about 970 mg per stick and LMNT about 1,000 mg. You won't notice a 30 mg difference.

What matters more is how much water you mix it into, because that decides how salty each sip is:

- **Either one in 16 ounces (about half a liter):** roughly 85 to 90 millimoles of sodium per liter. That's saltier than the World Health Organization's oral rehydration solution, which sits at 75. Most people find it strong at this dilution.
- **Either one in 32 ounces (about a liter):** roughly 42 to 45 millimoles per liter, close to what a stick of Liquid I.V. gives in 16 ounces.

If you find either one too salty, the fix is more water.

### How much sodium is too much?

US dietary guidelines suggest most adults keep sodium under about 2,300 mg a day, and the American Heart Association points to 1,500 mg as an ideal target for many adults, especially those with high blood pressure. One stick of either brand uses up about 40% of that 2,300 mg figure before you've eaten anything.

For a healthy person who sweats a lot, or someone on a strict low-carb diet (which makes the kidneys shed more sodium), that can be reasonable. For someone sitting at a desk all day eating a normal diet, it's a lot of extra salt. Neither of these is a "sip it all day" drink for most people. If you want a deeper look at sodium-heavy versus sugar-based mixes, see our [LMNT vs Liquid I.V. comparison](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv).

## Potassium: SALTT Has About Twice as Much

This is the first real difference. SALTT has about 410 mg of potassium per stick, while LMNT has about 200 mg.

Potassium works alongside sodium to keep fluid balance, nerve signals, and muscle contractions running normally. Most adults in the US eat less potassium than recommended, so a bit more from a drink mix is usually fine, and for many people it's a plus. As a reference point, the WHO's oral rehydration formula has 20 millimoles of potassium per liter. A stick of SALTT in 16 ounces of water lands right around that. LMNT in the same amount of water gives about half.

The catch is that potassium is the electrolyte doctors worry about most in certain people. Healthy kidneys get rid of extra potassium easily. Kidneys that aren't working well can't, and some common medicines (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone) also make the body hold on to it. In those situations, extra potassium can build up to levels that affect the heart rhythm. **If you have kidney disease or take one of those medicines, ask your doctor before using SALTT or any potassium-containing electrolyte mix regularly.** SALTT itself sells a lower-potassium drops product for people who want to limit it.

## Magnesium: SALTT Has About Three Times as Much

This is the biggest difference on paper. SALTT has about 180 mg of magnesium per stick. LMNT has about 60 mg.

Magnesium helps with muscle and nerve function, energy production, and sleep regulation, and a lot of adults don't get enough from food. People on low-carb diets sometimes notice cramps or poor sleep that improves with more magnesium, which is part of why SALTT leans into it.

There are two things to know:

1. **More magnesium can mean looser stools.** The US National Institutes of Health sets an upper limit of 350 mg a day for magnesium from supplements (not food) in adults, mainly because higher doses commonly cause diarrhea and cramping. Two sticks of SALTT gets you to about 360 mg. Add a magnesium pill at bedtime and you're well over. LMNT's lower dose leaves much more room.
2. **Kidney disease matters here too.** Like potassium, magnesium is cleared by the kidneys. People with kidney problems should get a doctor's OK before taking extra.

If you already take a magnesium supplement, LMNT fits more easily into your day. If you don't, SALTT's dose is a convenient way to cover a good chunk of your daily needs, as long as your stomach handles it.

## Sugar and Sweeteners: The Same Approach

Neither product has sugar, and both use stevia to sweeten the flavored versions. Both also sell an unsweetened, unflavored option: SALTT's "Clean Slate" and LMNT's "Raw." Those taste like salty water and are mostly for people avoiding sweeteners or adding the salt to food or other drinks.

Being sugar-free is the whole point for keto and fasting crowds. But it's worth understanding the trade-off. Classic oral rehydration drinks include a small amount of glucose on purpose. Glucose and sodium are absorbed together through the same transporter in the small intestine, and water follows. That's why the WHO formula pairs them. A sugar-free mix still delivers sodium and still helps you hold on to the water you drink, but it doesn't use that glucose shortcut. For everyday hydration that makes little difference. For someone who is genuinely dehydrated, nauseous, and struggling to keep fluids down, a little sugar can help.

## Taste and Flavors

Taste is personal, so take this as a general guide rather than a verdict.

- **Both are salty.** If you're coming from Gatorade or Liquid I.V., the first sip of either will surprise you, especially in 16 ounces of water.
- **SALTT can taste a little more mineral.** Magnesium salts have a slightly bitter edge, and SALTT has three times as much. Some people notice it, some don't. Flavors with stronger fruit or chocolate notes hide it better.
- **LMNT is a bit cleaner-tasting** for some people because of its lower magnesium, though it's still unmistakably salty.
- **Both have chocolate and citrus options.** Both brands offer fruit flavors and a chocolate flavor meant for mixing into hot water or milk, and both rotate seasonal flavors.

The easiest way to decide is to buy a variety pack of one, try it in 24 to 32 ounces of water, and adjust from there.

## Price and Value

At the time of writing, SALTT generally runs around $1.20 per stick, and LMNT about $1.50 per stick at full price, with discounts for bulk boxes and subscriptions. Prices change, so check the current numbers.

If you measure value by minerals per dollar, SALTT wins clearly: similar sodium, double the potassium, triple the magnesium, for less money. If you only care about sodium, the gap narrows to price alone.

There's also a cheaper route for either: you can make a basic salty drink at home with table salt, a salt substitute that contains potassium chloride, and a squeeze of citrus. It won't taste as good and it's easy to get the amounts wrong, so it's best for people who know exactly what they want. If you have any of the health conditions listed above, don't use potassium salt substitutes without your doctor's OK.

## SALTT vs LMNT for Keto and Fasting

This is the use case both brands were built for, and both do the job well.

On a strict low-carb diet, insulin levels drop and the kidneys release more sodium and water, especially in the first couple of weeks. That's a big reason for the headaches, fatigue, and cramps people call "keto flu." Getting more sodium usually helps, and enough potassium and magnesium helps too.

- **SALTT** covers all three minerals more fully, which is why it's popular with people who don't want a separate magnesium pill.
- **LMNT** covers sodium just as well but leaves you to get more potassium and magnesium from food (avocado, leafy greens, nuts) or a supplement.

During a fast, both are zero-sugar and very low in calories. Whether stevia "breaks" a fast depends on how strict you are and why you're fasting. Many people use them while fasting without a problem. If you're strict, both brands offer an unsweetened version.

## SALTT vs LMNT for Workouts and Heavy Sweating

For long, sweaty sessions, hot weather, or people who end a workout with salt crusted on their clothes, sodium is the main thing to replace, and the two are almost identical there. Pick based on taste and price.

For very long endurance events (think several hours), many athletes also need carbohydrates for fuel. Neither SALTT nor LMNT provides any, so you'd pair them with food, gels, or a sports drink. For a normal hour at the gym, most people don't need an electrolyte drink at all. Water and a normal meal afterward are fine.

## SALTT vs LMNT for a Hangover

People often reach for an electrolyte drink the morning after, so it's worth being clear about what these can and can't do.

### What alcohol actually does to fluids

Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With it suppressed, you urinate more than you drink, which is why you can wake up thirsty with a dry mouth. If you also vomited or sweated a lot, you lost sodium and potassium too. Regular heavy drinking is also known to lower magnesium levels over time, because alcohol increases how much magnesium the kidneys flush out.

### Why an electrolyte drink only helps part of the problem

Dehydration is real after drinking, but it's only one piece of a hangover. Researchers who have studied hangovers point to several other drivers: an inflammatory response, poor-quality sleep, the effects of acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product made when your body breaks down alcohol), and changes in blood sugar. Studies that measured electrolytes in hungover people have generally not found large disturbances, and hangover severity doesn't track closely with how dehydrated someone is. Rehydrating can help you feel less awful, but there is no good evidence that any electrolyte drink, including SALTT or LMNT, cures or prevents a hangover.

### Which one is better the morning after?

- **If you're just thirsty and a bit foggy:** either is fine. Mix one stick into a full 32 ounces and sip it over an hour or two along with some food.
- **If you're nauseous or have been vomiting:** a sugar-containing oral rehydration drink is usually the better choice, because the glucose helps your gut absorb water and sodium, and a less salty drink is easier to keep down in small sips. Our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) ranks the options for this.
- **If you have a sensitive stomach:** be cautious with SALTT's higher magnesium. Alcohol already irritates the gut, and a big dose of magnesium on top can make loose stools worse. Half a stick in a full glass is a gentler start.

For more on timing, see our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking). For why drinking drains fluid and salts in the first place, see [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

### When to see a doctor

Most hangovers pass on their own within a day. But get medical help if you or someone you're with has:

- Vomiting that won't stop, or can't keep any fluids down for many hours
- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, trouble staying awake, or slow or irregular breathing (these can be signs of alcohol poisoning, so call 911)
- Very little or no urine for a long stretch, or very dark urine that doesn't improve with fluids
- A racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, chest pain, or fainting
- Muscle weakness or cramps that are severe or getting worse

Don't try to fix any of these with an electrolyte drink. They need proper care.

## Who Should Be Careful With Either One

Both products pack a lot of minerals into a small stick. Check with a doctor before regular use if you:

- Have **high blood pressure** or have been told to limit salt
- Have **kidney disease** of any stage, since your kidneys may not clear extra potassium and magnesium well
- Have **heart failure** or have been told to limit fluids
- Take **ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, or other potassium-sparing diuretics**, which can raise potassium on their own (SALTT's higher potassium matters most here)
- Take **water pills (diuretics)** of any type, since they change sodium and potassium balance
- Take a **magnesium supplement** or magnesium-containing laxatives or antacids (SALTT's higher magnesium matters most here)
- Are **pregnant**, or giving these to a **child**

For healthy adults using one stick a day, both are generally well tolerated. The risks come from stacking several sticks, combining them with other supplements, or having a health condition that affects how your body handles these minerals.

## How to Use Either One Sensibly

- **Start with one stick a day,** in 24 to 32 ounces of water.
- **Use more water, not more sticks,** if it tastes too strong.
- **Count your other sources.** Salty food, other electrolyte drinks, and magnesium supplements all add up.
- **Match it to your day.** A sweaty workout, a hot day, a low-carb diet, or a night of drinking can justify one. A normal desk day usually doesn't.
- **Watch your stomach.** Loose stools after SALTT are a sign the magnesium is too much for you. Cut back to half a stick.

## The Verdict

- **Choose SALTT** if you want the most complete mineral profile and the best value, you eat low-carb or fast, and you don't already take a magnesium supplement.
- **Choose LMNT** if you mainly want sodium, prefer a gentler magnesium dose, already supplement magnesium, or want the brand that's easier to find in stores.
- **Choose neither on its own** if you're nauseous and dehydrated after a rough night or a stomach bug. A sugar-containing oral rehydration drink is the better tool there.

## A Note on Hangover Prevention

If you're comparing electrolyte mixes because you regularly wake up rough after drinking, rehydration is only one part of the picture. The habits with the best evidence are the simple ones: drink less, drink slower, eat a real meal beforehand, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers them.

Some people also add DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also does nothing to replace fluids, so it isn't a substitute for an electrolyte drink. If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking and good hydration, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is SALTT or LMNT better?**

Neither is better for everyone. They have nearly the same sodium (about 970 mg vs 1,000 mg per stick) and no sugar. SALTT has about twice the potassium and three times the magnesium and usually costs less per stick. LMNT has a gentler magnesium dose and is easier to find. Choose SALTT for the fullest mineral dose and value, and LMNT if you already take magnesium or have a sensitive stomach.

**Which has more magnesium, SALTT or LMNT?**

SALTT, by a wide margin. A stick of SALTT has about 180 mg of magnesium, compared with about 60 mg in LMNT. The NIH upper limit for magnesium from supplements is 350 mg a day for adults, mainly because more can cause diarrhea, so two sticks of SALTT plus a magnesium pill can put you over it.

**Is SALTT or LMNT better for a hangover?**

Either can help with thirst and mild dehydration, but neither cures or prevents a hangover. If you're nauseous or have been vomiting, a sugar-containing oral rehydration drink is usually the better choice, because glucose helps your gut absorb water and sodium. If you use SALTT or LMNT, mix one stick into a full 32 ounces and sip it slowly with food. SALTT's higher magnesium can be harder on an already upset stomach.

**Is SALTT cheaper than LMNT?**

Usually, yes. At the time of writing, SALTT runs around $1.20 per stick and LMNT about $1.50 at full price, with discounts for bulk orders and subscriptions on both. Prices change, so check the current numbers before buying.

**Are SALTT and LMNT good for keto?**

Yes. Both are sugar-free and very low in calories, and both were designed with low-carb diets in mind. Low-carb eating makes the kidneys release more sodium, which contributes to "keto flu," and a gram of sodium a day from either can help. SALTT also covers more of your potassium and magnesium needs.

**Can you drink SALTT or LMNT every day?**

Most healthy adults can use one stick a day without trouble, especially if they sweat a lot or eat low-carb. Each stick has about 40% of the US daily sodium limit of 2,300 mg, so several a day adds up fast. People with high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure, or who take blood pressure medicines or water pills, should ask a doctor before using either regularly.

**Who should not drink SALTT?**

Check with a doctor first if you have kidney disease, take ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone, already take a magnesium supplement, or have been told to limit salt or potassium. SALTT's higher potassium and magnesium are fine for most healthy people but matter more in these situations.

**Does LMNT or SALTT break a fast?**

Both have zero sugar and only a few calories, so for most fasting goals they're generally considered fine. If you follow a very strict fast and want to avoid sweeteners entirely, both brands sell an unsweetened, unflavored version: SALTT's Clean Slate and LMNT's Raw.
